problem_motivation.content: Choosing optimal reactive-element dopants in high-entropy alloys is still empirical because the thermodynamic landscape cannot be accessed at sufficient compositional resolution by first-principles methods.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Selecting optimal RE dopants in high-entropy alloys remains empirical because the relevant thermodynamic landscape is inaccessible to first-principles at the required compositional resolution.

problem_motivation.content: Oxide-scale adhesion in HEAs is a central deployment challenge because scale failure causes accelerated degradation.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Understanding and predicting the adhesion of oxide scales to HEA substrates is therefore a central challenge for the deployment of these materials.

problem_motivation.content: Choosing reactive elements for specific alloy-oxide systems remains empirical.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Despite decades of research, RE selection for a given alloy–oxide com-bination remains largely empirical.

problem_motivation.content: The alloy/RE/oxide/composition design space is too large for exhaustive experiments.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: With six principal elements, five RE candidates, two oxide types, and continuous composition ranges, the design space is inaccessible to exhaustive experimental exploration.

prior_approach.content: Experimental studies established oxidation behavior across key HEA families.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Extensive experimental work has established the oxidation phenomenology of key HEA families.

prior_approach.content: Reactive-element additions have been used to counteract sulfur effects.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The addition of REs such as Hf and Y at trace levels counteracts sulfur

prior_approach.content: First-principles DFT has been used to study specific systems.
prior_approach.evidence_span: First-principles density functional theory has provided valuable atomistic insight for specific systems [25–28]

prior_approach.content: The authors previously extended the macroscopic atom model to multicomponent alloys and validated it against DFT.
prior_approach.evidence_span: In our previous paper [29], we extended the macroscopic atom model (MAM) [30, 31] to multicomponent alloys, where we validated the framework against DFT for CoCrFeNi and Al-CoCrFeNi systems.

prior_limitation.content: First-principles methods cannot access the relevant thermodynamic landscape at the needed compositional resolution.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: the relevant thermodynamic landscape is inaccessible to first-principles at the required compositional resolution

prior_limitation.content: DFT interface supercell calculations are too costly to cover more than isolated configurations.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: but the computational cost of interface supercell calcula-tions limits coverage to isolated configurations.

prior_limitation.content: The model neglects graded composition profiles and non-stoichiometric defects in real oxide scales.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: neglecting the graded composition profiles and non-stoichiometric defects present in real oxide scales [9, 11].

prior_limitation.content: Treating the oxide as a pseudo-alloy overestimates oxide surface energy relative to experiment.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: the MAM computes oxide surface energies by treating the ox-ide as a pseudo-alloy of its metallic and non-metallic constituents, which overestimates γoxide relative to experimental values.

inspiration_source.content: Percolation-threshold concept from passive-film formation is used to interpret Cr dependence of adhesion
inspiration_source.evidence_span: The dominance of Cr as the adhesion lever at Cr2 O3 connects to the percolation threshold concept. Xie et al. [41] showed that a minimum of ∼10–12 at% Cr is required for continuous passive film formation

inspiration_source.content: A prior review identifying AlCoCrFeNi with refractory additions as promising is supported quantitatively here
inspiration_source.evidence_span: The review by Veselkov et al. [13] concluded that AlCoCrFeNi alloys with additions of refractory elements represent the most promising direction for oxidation-resistant HEAs; the present analysis provides a quantitative thermodynamic basis for this recommendation.

inspiration_source.content: Aqueous corrosion work on selective oxidation and Ni-rich subsurface is used as an analogy to high-temperature oxidation effects
inspiration_source.evidence_span: Chen et al. [24] showed that selective oxidation in Al0.1 CrCoFeNi during corrosion alters the subsurface composition in a manner analogous to high-temperature oxidation

causal_claim.content: The oxide-dependent ranking inversion is caused by the interplay between reactive-element–oxygen and reactive-element–matrix interaction enthalpies.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The screening reveals an oxide-dependent ranking inversion, with Hf dominating at Cr2 O3 and La dominating at Al2 O3 , driven by the interplay between RE–O and RE–matrix interaction enthalpies.

causal_claim.content: Sulfur segregation to the interface weakens adhesion and promotes spallation even below 30 ppm bulk sulfur.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Sulfur at bulk concentrations below 30 ppm can accumulate at oxide–metal inter-faces to levels sufficient to weaken adhesion and promote spallation

causal_claim.content: Selective oxidation causes a Ni-enriched subsurface layer that hinders repassivation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: selective oxi-dation of Cr, Co, and Fe in Al0.1 CrCoFeNi creates a Ni-enriched subsurface layer that hinders repassivation

causal_claim.content: Because the oxide-surface-energy error is a constant offset for a given oxide, relative rankings and trends are unaffected.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Since this enters Wsep as a constant additive offset for all alloys at a given oxide, all inter-alloy rankings, ∆Wsep enhancements, segregation enthalpies, and crossover con-centrations are unaffected

causal_claim.content: Low surface enthalpy of Al lowers alloy surface energies
causal_claim.evidence_span: Al-containing alloys consistently exhibit lower surface energies by 0.2–0.3 J/m2 , reflecting the low surface enthalpy of Al

causal_claim.content: Mn lowers surface energy in Mn-containing variants
causal_claim.evidence_span: the Cantor alloy (2.28 J/m2 ) lies below CoCrFeNi (2.46 J/m2 ) due to Mn’s lower surface enthalpy.

causal_claim.content: Cross-interface chemistry, not surface energies, mainly differentiates adhesion
causal_claim.evidence_span: Because the alloy surface energy enters both the numerator of Wsep and the interfacial energy term with partially canceling contributions, the cross-interface chemical interactions, rather than the surface energies themselves, emerge as the dominant factor differentiating adhesion across families

causal_claim.content: Stronger Cr–O bonding gives chromia interfaces higher adhesion
causal_claim.evidence_span: This systematic advantage arises primarily from the stronger Cr–O cross-interface bonding (∆H ◦ = −578 kJ/mol) relative to the Al–O interactions already present within the alumina lattice

causal_claim.content: Strong Al–Cr interaction raises adhesion at chromia interfaces
causal_claim.evidence_span: Al increases Wsep at Cr2 O3 (CoCrFeNi: 5.90 → AlCoCrFeNi: 5.93 J/m2 ) through the strong Al–Cr interaction

causal_claim.content: At alumina, Al decreases adhesion
causal_claim.evidence_span: while decreasing it at Al2 O3 (5.46 → 5.36 J/m2 ) because like-element contacts across the interface contribute nothing to the chemical bonding.

causal_claim.content: Weaker Mn–O interaction causes the Mn-induced adhesion penalty
causal_claim.evidence_span: This reduction of 0.06–0.08 J/m2 arises from the weaker Mn–O interaction

causal_claim.content: Rapid outward Mn diffusion creates Kirkendall porosity and further weakens adhesion
causal_claim.evidence_span: The rapid outward Mn diffusion creates Kirkendall porosity [11], further weakening adhesion through mechanical void-mediated decohesion

causal_claim.content: The chromia segregation ordering is set by solute–oxide attraction balanced against bulk penalty
causal_claim.evidence_span: This ordering reflects the balance between the solute–oxide attraction (Term 1) and the solute–bulk penalty (Term 3)

causal_claim.content: La ranks lower because large molar volume creates mismatch penalty
causal_claim.evidence_span: La ranks fourth because its large molar volume (VLa = 22.55 cm3 /mol) creates an unfavorable mismatch contribution.

causal_claim.content: Ranking inversion originates from stronger La interaction with Al-dominated oxide than Hf at alumina
causal_claim.evidence_span: The inversion originates in Term 1: La’s interaction with the Al-dominated oxide (−1.52 eV) exceeds that of Hf (−1.38 eV) at Al2 O3

causal_claim.content: La mismatch penalty is too small to overturn its alumina advantage
causal_claim.evidence_span: The mismatch penalty for La (Term 4: +0.24 eV) is constant across oxide types and insufficient to reverse the ranking at Al2 O3 .

causal_claim.content: Ti's favorable matrix interactions reduce its net segregation drive
causal_claim.evidence_span: Ti’s favorable matrix interactions reduce the net segregation driving force

causal_claim.content: Weaker sulfur segregation in Al-containing alloys reduces sulfur sensitivity
causal_claim.evidence_span: This reduced sensitivity of Al-containing alloys correlates with their weaker S segregation enthalpies: less S reaches the interface at equilibrium, and the interfacial bonding network is less disrupted per unit of S coverage.

causal_claim.content: Absence of Ni lowers crossover concentrations by removing competition for interfacial sites
causal_claim.evidence_span: The absence of Ni, which competes with REs for interfacial sites, removes a key impediment to RE segregation.

causal_claim.content: CoCrFeMn is easiest to protect because Mn weakens sulfur segregation while Hf remains strongly interfacially segregating
causal_claim.evidence_span: CoCrFeMn is the easiest alloy to protect because its strong Mn–S bulk interaction weakens S segregation (∆HsegS = −0.22 eV), while Hf maintains strong interfacial segregation (−1.01 eV).

causal_claim.content: CoCrFeNi + Ti is hardest because sulfur segregates strongly and Ti segregates weakly
causal_claim.evidence_span: CoCrFeNi has the strongest S segregation among all families (−0.46 eV at Cr2 O3 ), and Ti’s relatively weak segregation (−0.80 eV) provides the smallest thermodynamic advantage over S.

causal_claim.content: Higher temperature reduces RE/S selectivity, raising crossover concentration
causal_claim.evidence_span: higher temperatures reduce the Boltzmann selectivity between RE and S.

causal_claim.content: RE choice adds a nearly uniform shift while composition governs map topology
causal_claim.evidence_span: The RE choice produces a uniform vertical shift (∼0.02 J/m2 ) without altering the contour topology, confirming that composition and RE effects are approximately separable at trace concentrations.

causal_claim.content: Adhesion enhancement depends on RE–O bond strength after segregation, not just segregation tendency
causal_claim.evidence_span: This distinction arises because ∆Wsep depends on the RE–O interaction enthalpy once the RE reaches the interface ... not on the thermodynamic driving force for getting there.

causal_claim.content: High effectiveness index in Al-containing alloys at chromia is amplified by near-zero sulfur segregation
causal_claim.evidence_span: The Al-containing alloys at Cr2 O3 exhibit elevated η values because their near-zero S segregation in the denominator amplifies the index

causal_claim.content: Mn lowers adhesion by diluting stronger metal–oxygen bonds with weaker Mn–O bonds
causal_claim.evidence_span: reflecting the dilution of stronger metal–O bonds by the weaker Mn–O interaction.

causal_claim.content: Strong Mn–S bulk interaction traps sulfur in the alloy and opposes interfacial segregation
causal_claim.evidence_span: This strong Mn–S bulk interaction creates a thermodynamic trap that stabilizes S in the alloy matrix and penalizes its migration to the interface.

causal_claim.content: Mn–O interaction drives outward diffusion and weak interfacial Mn–O bonding gives poorly anchored scale
causal_claim.evidence_span: the Mn–O interaction provides the driving force for outward diffusion, while the weak Mn–O bond at the interface ensures that the resulting scale is poorly anchored.

causal_claim.content: Combined Al and Mn sulfur trapping creates sulfur immunity threshold
causal_claim.evidence_span: This threshold arises from the combined S-trapping effect of Al ... and Mn

causal_claim.content: Alloy composition, RE choice, and oxide type reduce to one thermodynamic parameter for crossover concentration
causal_claim.evidence_span: The entire complexity of alloy composition, RE choice, and oxide type reduces to a single thermodynamic parameter.

causal_claim.content: High Al content gives sulfur immunity and strong adhesion through sulfur trapping and favorable Al–O bonding
causal_claim.evidence_span: The high Al content creates both a strong Al–S bulk trap and favorable Al–O cross-interface bonding.

causal_claim.content: Strong bonding maintains contact and resists delamination during scale growth
causal_claim.evidence_span: because strong bonding resists delamination and maintains intimate contact during growth.

causal_claim.content: Kirkendall voids from outward Mn diffusion further reduce practical adhesion
causal_claim.evidence_span: Vacancy condensation from preferential outward Mn diffusion creates voids that reduce the effective contact area, further decreasing practical adhesion below the thermodynamic Wsep .

mechanism_principle.content: Interplay between reactive-element–oxygen and reactive-element–matrix interaction enthalpies explains the ranking inversion.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: driven by the interplay between RE–O and RE–matrix interaction enthalpies

mechanism_principle.content: The universal crossover behavior is governed by the segregation enthalpy difference.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: governed by the segrega- tion enthalpy difference

mechanism_principle.content: Reactive elements act by competitively displacing sulfur, modifying oxide growth, and forming anchoring RE–O pegs.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: through competitive interfacial displacement, modification of oxide growth kinetics, and formation of stable RE–O pegs that anchor the scale

mechanism_principle.content: Segregation enthalpy is modeled as arising from oxide attraction, disruption of interfacial bonding, bulk removal cost, and elastic strain from size mismatch.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The first term in brackets of Eq. (3) captures the chemical attraction between the solute and the oxide surface, the second term represents the bonding across the clean interface that must be disrupted when the solute replaces a matrix atom, and the third term accounts for the energy cost of removing the solute from the bulk alloy; the last term captures the elastic strain energy from the size mismatch between solute and host.

mechanism_principle.content: The model is most predictive for relative comparisons rather than absolute adhesion energies because the oxide-energy error is a constant additive offset.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Since this enters Wsep as a constant additive offset for all alloys at a given oxide, all inter-alloy rankings, ∆Wsep enhancements, segregation enthalpies, and crossover con-centrations are unaffected; the model’s predictive strength therefore lies in relative comparisons rather than absolute adhesion energies.

mechanism_principle.content: Preferential Al surface enrichment explains the surface-energy trend
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This trend is consistent with the predicted preferential surface enrichment of Al by the Gibbs adsorption isotherm.

mechanism_principle.content: Partial cancellation of surface-energy contributions makes cross-interface interactions dominant
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Because the alloy surface energy enters both the numerator of Wsep and the interfacial energy term with partially canceling contributions

mechanism_principle.content: Chromia gains from stronger cross-interface Cr–O bonds, unlike alumina where Al–O is already internal to the lattice
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: from the stronger Cr–O cross-interface bonding (∆H ◦ = −578 kJ/mol) relative to the Al–O interactions already present within the alumina lattice

mechanism_principle.content: Like-element contacts across alumina interfaces do not add chemical bonding
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: because like-element contacts across the interface contribute nothing to the chemical bonding

mechanism_principle.content: Mn–O bonds are weaker than competing metal–O bonds
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: arises from the weaker Mn–O interaction (−520 kJ/mol) relative to Cr–O (−578), Co–O (−302), and Fe–O (−413 kJ/mol).

mechanism_principle.content: Model explains Mn effect through weaker Mn–O cross-interface bonds
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The model attributes the adhesion reduction to weaker Mn–O cross-interface bonds

mechanism_principle.content: Void-mediated decohesion from Kirkendall porosity amplifies thermodynamic adhesion weakness
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: further weakening adhesion through mechanical void-mediated decohesion, thereby amplifying the thermodynamic weakness predicted here.

mechanism_principle.content: Y ranks second because weaker Y–O bonding is offset by more favorable matrix interactions
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: although the Y–O interaction (−953 kJ/mol) is weaker than Hf–O (−1113 kJ/mol), Y’s more favorable matrix interactions partially compensate, placing it second.

mechanism_principle.content: More exothermic La–Al interaction drives La dominance at alumina, while reverse chemistry holds at chromia
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: driven by the more exothermic La–Al interaction (∆HLaAl = −231 kJ/mol vs. Hf–Al: −215 kJ/mol), while the reverse holds at Cr2 O3 (∆HLaCr = +93 kJ/mol).

mechanism_principle.content: Lower equilibrium sulfur coverage and less bond-network disruption explain reduced sulfur sensitivity
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: less S reaches the interface at equilibrium, and the interfacial bonding network is less disrupted per unit of S coverage.

mechanism_principle.content: Excess RE is needed to overcome kinetic and microstructural losses
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The excess serves primarily to compensate for kinetic limitations including slow bulk diffusion of RE to the interface, consumption by internal oxidation, and RE sequestration at grain boundaries

mechanism_principle.content: Strong Mn–S bulk binding suppresses sulfur segregation, while strong Hf segregation favors protection
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: because its strong Mn–S bulk interaction weakens S segregation ... while Hf maintains strong interfacial segregation

mechanism_principle.content: Boltzmann-factor amplification strongly favors RE enrichment over sulfur
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: the exponential amplification from the Boltzmann factor overwhelmingly favors RE enrichment.

mechanism_principle.content: Approximate separability allows independent optimization of base composition and RE
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This separability means that alloy designers can first optimize the base composition for adhesion, then independently select the RE.

mechanism_principle.content: Segregation tendency and bond-strength enhancement are distinct properties
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The element that segregates most readily is not necessarily the one that strengthens the interface most.

mechanism_principle.content: Near-zero sulfur segregation makes little RE intervention sufficient for protection
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: reflecting the physical reality that these alloys require minimal RE intervention for S protection.

mechanism_principle.content: Mn has a double-edged role: weaker oxide bonding but better sulfur gettering
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Mn thus presents a double-edged character where it weakens the oxide–metal bond while simultaneously protecting the interface from S poisoning.

mechanism_principle.content: Al–S and Mn–S interactions are more exothermic than Ni–S, Co–S, or Cr–S, stabilizing sulfur in the bulk
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: both more exothermic than the Ni–S, Co–S, or Cr–S interactions.

mechanism_principle.content: Combined low intrinsic adhesion and void-reduced contact area explains severe Cantor-alloy spallation
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The combination of lower intrinsic adhesion and void-mediated area reduction explains the severe spallation observed in the Cantor alloy.

hypothesis_statement.content: The authors propose using the macroscopic atom model with McLean isotherm and Guttmann models to screen oxide-scale adhesion across alloy families and reactive elements.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Here we apply the macroscopic atom model, coupled with McLean isotherm and Guttmann models, to screen adhesion across nine CoCrFeMnNiAl sub-families at Cr2 O3 and Al2 O3 interfaces, ranking five REs (Hf, Y, Zr, La, Ti) for segregation, adhesion enhancement, and sulfur displacement.

hypothesis_statement.content: The present work applies the extended MAM to screen adhesion and rank reactive elements across CoCrFeMnNiAl sub-families and oxide interfaces.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Here we apply this framework to screen adhesion across nine sub-families of the CoCrFeMnNiAl system at both Cr2 O3 and Al2 O3 in-terfaces, ranking five REs for segregation tendency, adhesion enhancement, and sulfur displacement, and systematically comparing the predictions with the experimental oxidation literature.

hypothesis_statement.content: Different reactive elements should be selected for chromia- versus alumina-forming alloys
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Hf should be preferred for chromia-forming alloys, while La or Y should be preferred for alumina-forming compositions.

hypothesis_statement.content: La may outperform Y/Hf at alumina and should be tested experimentally
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: However, the model suggests that La alone could have provided even stronger interfacial enrichment at Al2 O3 (−1.29 eV), a prediction that warrants experimental verification.

hypothesis_statement.content: The paper proposes a composite RE effectiveness index combining segregation and bond-strength effects
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: To provide a single-metric ranking, we define a dimensionless composite RE effectiveness index that combines both

hypothesis_statement.content: Mn-containing compositions may be good RE-doped hosts because low RE levels can displace sulfur while Mn adds intrinsic sulfur resistance
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Mn-containing compositions like CoCrFeMn or CrFeMnNi may be effective hosts for RE doping requiring the lowest RE concentrations for S displacement while providing inherent S resistance as a secondary protection mechanism.

hypothesis_statement.content: Near-zero or positive sulfur segregation motivates constructing a sulfur-immunity phase diagram
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: The observation that certain Al- and Mn-containing alloys exhibit near-zero or positive S segregation enthalpies motivates the construction of a sulfur immunity phase diagram.

hypothesis_statement.content: All crossover data should collapse onto a master curve versus segregation-enthalpy difference
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Eq. (5) predicts that all crossover concentrations should collapse onto a single master curve when plotted against the segregation enthalpy difference

hypothesis_statement.content: Inverse design seeks compositions that maximize adhesion while remaining sulfur-immune
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: The natural convergence of the S immunity boundary and the adhesion maps raises the question: what composition simultaneously achieves S immunity and maximum adhesion?

hypothesis_statement.content: Moderately elevated Al with some Mn may achieve sulfur immunity while retaining FCC-based structure
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Non-equiatomic variants with moderately elevated Al (15–25 at%) combined with 10–15 at% Mn could potentially achieve S immunity while maintaining an FCC-based structure.

hypothesis_statement.content: Adhesion maps can predict how oxidation-induced compositional perturbations shift adhesion over spallation-regrowth cycles
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: The adhesion maps presented here (Fig. 9) provide a framework for predicting how such compositional perturbations shift Wsep and would affect adhesion after multiple spallation–regrowth cycles.

evidence_result.content: Screening found an oxide-dependent inversion in dopant ranking, with Hf best at Cr2O3 and La best at Al2O3.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The screening reveals an oxide-dependent ranking inversion, with Hf dominating at Cr2 O3 and La dominat- ing at Al2 O3

evidence_result.content: Mn-containing alloys show intrinsic sulfur resistance consistent with experimental oxidation behavior.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Mn-containing alloys exhibit intrinsic sulfur resistance, con- sistent with their experimentally observed oxidation characteristics.

evidence_result.content: A phase diagram indicates compositions with aluminum plus manganese at or above about 25 at% are thermodynamically immune to sulfur-induced adhesion loss.
evidence_result.evidence_span: A sulfur immunity phase diagram identifies compositions with Al + Mn ≳ 25 at% as thermodynamically immune to S-induced adhesion loss.

evidence_result.content: All crossover concentrations follow a universal exponential relation governed by the segregation enthalpy difference.
evidence_result.evidence_span: All crossover con- centrations collapse onto a universal exponential governed by the segrega- tion enthalpy difference, providing a transferable design rule.

evidence_result.content: Inverse design identified Co16Cr16Fe16Ni16Al35 as the best sulfur-immune composition without reactive-element doping, with separation work 5.95 J/m2.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Inverse design identifies Co16 Cr16 Fe16 Ni16 Al35 as the optimal S-immune composition with Wsep = 5.95 J/m2 without RE doping.

evidence_result.content: Laplanche et al. found Mn-rich oxides dominate oxidation in the Cantor alloy, with activation energy controlled by Mn diffusion through oxide.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Laplanche et al. [9] showed that Mn-rich oxides (α-Mn2 O3 at 600–800◦ C, Mn3 O4 at 900◦ C) dominate the scale, with an oxidation activation energy of 130 ± 10 kJ/mol controlled by Mn diffusion through the oxide rather than sluggish diffusion in the alloy matrix [10].

evidence_result.content: Mn-free CoCrFeNi forms a more continuous, better-adherent oxide and oxidizes an order of magnitude more slowly than the Cantor alloy, while Cr-free CoFeMnNi oxidizes catastrophically.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Dehury et al. [11] extended these observations to 30-day exposures at 1000◦ C, demonstrating that Mn-free CoCrFeNi forms a more continuous, better-adherent oxide with an oxidation rate constant one order of magnitude lower than that of the Cantor alloy, while Cr-free CoFeMnNi undergoes catastrophic oxidation with phase decomposition.

evidence_result.content: Low-Mn, high-Cr variants showed the best scale retention.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Holcomb et al. [7] confirmed this hierarchy across eight CoCrFeMnNi variants, finding that low-Mn, high-Cr compositions exhibited the best scale retention.

evidence_result.content: At least 20 at% Al promotes continuous protective alumina.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Butler and Weaver [12] showed that ≥20 at% Al promotes continuous protective Al2 O3

evidence_result.content: Trace Y and Hf co-doping yields a thin uniform alpha-alumina scale after long exposure.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Lu et al. [4] demonstrated that co-doping AlCoCrFeNi with only 0.02 at% each of Y and Hf produces a uniform α-Al2 O3 scale just 4.6 µm thick after 1000 h at 1100◦ C.

evidence_result.content: Reviews conclude Al and Cr favor protective oxide formation, whereas Mn worsens oxidation resistance.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Comprehensive reviews [13] have concluded that Al and Cr are the most im-portant elements for protective oxide formation, while Mn degrades oxidation resistance through porous, poorly adhering scale phases.

evidence_result.content: Selective oxidation in Al0.1CrCoFeNi creates a Ni-enriched subsurface layer that hinders repassivation.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Chen et al. [24] further demonstrated that selective oxi-dation of Cr, Co, and Fe in Al0.1 CrCoFeNi creates a Ni-enriched subsurface layer that hinders repassivation

evidence_result.content: Validation against DFT showed the MAM reproduces segregation hierarchies and adhesion trends.
evidence_result.evidence_span: validation against DFT [29] demonstrates that the MAM correctly reproduces segregation hierarchies and adhesion trends, providing a reliable basis for comparative screening.

evidence_result.content: Al-containing alloys have lower computed surface energies than Al-free alloys
evidence_result.evidence_span: Al-containing alloys consistently exhibit lower surface energies by 0.2–0.3 J/m2

evidence_result.content: Predicted CoCrFeNi surface energy agrees with DFT
evidence_result.evidence_span: The predicted value for CoCrFeNi agrees well with DFT calculations reporting 2.3–2.6 J/m2 depending on crystallographic orientation [39].

evidence_result.content: Chromia interfaces show higher adhesion than alumina across all alloys
evidence_result.evidence_span: Chromia interfaces consistently produce higher Wsep than alumina across all alloy compositions (Fig. 2), with differences ranging from 0.43 J/m2 (Cantor) to 0.60 J/m2 (AlCrFeNi).

evidence_result.content: Al slightly increases adhesion at chromia but decreases it at alumina
evidence_result.evidence_span: Al increases Wsep at Cr2 O3 (CoCrFeNi: 5.90 → AlCoCrFeNi: 5.93 J/m2 ) through the strong Al–Cr interaction (∆HAlCr = −87 kJ/mol), while decreasing it at Al2 O3 (5.46 → 5.36 J/m2 )

evidence_result.content: Mn reduces adhesion at both oxide interfaces by about 0.06–0.08 J/m2
evidence_result.evidence_span: Mn systematically reduces Wsep at both interfaces: CoCrFeNi (5.90) → Cantor (5.82 J/m2 ), and AlCoCrFeNi (5.93) → AlCoCrFeMnNi (5.87 J/m2 ). This reduction of 0.06–0.08 J/m2

evidence_result.content: Experiments show worse oxidation/spallation for Mn-containing Cantor alloy than Mn-free CoCrFeNi
evidence_result.evidence_span: Dehury et al. [11] found that after 30 days at 1000◦ C, CoCrFeNi formed a relatively continuous oxide layer with good surface adherence, whereas CoCrFeMnNi exhibited a rough, discontinuous, and significantly spalled scale with Kirkendall pores at the metal–oxide interface. Their measured oxidation rate constant for CoCrFeNi (8.8 × 10−5 (mg/mm2 )3 /s) was approximately seven times lower than for CoCrFeMnNi (59 × 10−5 (mg/mm2 )3 /s).

evidence_result.content: Predicted adhesion hierarchy matches experimental oxidation rankings
evidence_result.evidence_span: The adhesion hierarchy predicted here, CoCrFeNi > CoCrFeMnNi ≫ CoFeMnNi, matches the experimental rankings at Cr2 O3 maps.

evidence_result.content: Experiments show Mn diffuses outward fastest and forms a fast-growing Mn-rich outer layer
evidence_result.evidence_span: experiments show that Mn diffuses outward through the oxide faster than any other element [7, 9, 11], forming a Mn-rich outer layer whose growth rate exceeds that of the parent alloy by an order of magnitude.

evidence_result.content: At chromia interfaces the segregation ranking is Hf > Y ≈ Zr > La > Ti across all families
evidence_result.evidence_span: At the Cr2 O3 interface, the ranking is remarkably consistent across all families: Hf > Y ≈ Zr > La > Ti.

evidence_result.content: At alumina interfaces La becomes the strongest segregant in most families
evidence_result.evidence_span: At the Al2 O3 interface, a dramatic ranking inversion occurs: La becomes the strongest segregant in most families, with Y second.

evidence_result.content: Prior co-doping experiment indirectly supports Y and Hf effectiveness at alumina
evidence_result.evidence_span: Lu et al. [4] achieved exceptional oxidation resistance in Y/Hf co-doped Al-CoCrFeNi, an alumina-forming alloy consistent with our prediction that both Y and Hf are effective at Al2 O3

evidence_result.content: Ti is consistently the weakest segregant
evidence_result.evidence_span: Ti consistently ranks weakest across all systems, with segregation enthalpies 30–50% below the strongest segregant.

evidence_result.content: All families lose adhesion monotonically as sulfur concentration increases
evidence_result.evidence_span: All families show monotonic adhesion decline with increasing S concentration

evidence_result.content: Al-containing alloys are less sensitive to sulfur-induced adhesion loss
evidence_result.evidence_span: CoCrFeNi and the Cantor alloy lose approximately 0.35 J/m2 of adhesion at 10 at% S surface fraction at Cr2 O3 , while AlCoCrFeNi loses only 0.20 J/m2 .

evidence_result.content: CoCrFeMn shows steep sulfur sensitivity but also the lowest RE crossover concentrations
evidence_result.evidence_span: The CoCrFeMn system shows the steepest decline in Wsep per unit S at Cr2 O3 ... this system also has the lowest crossover concentrations for RE displacement of S

evidence_result.content: All crossover concentrations are below 3 ppm and mostly below 1 ppm
evidence_result.evidence_span: all crossover concentrations for multicomponent HEAs are below 3 ppm at both interfaces, with the majority below 1 ppm.

evidence_result.content: Practical RE alloying levels exceed predicted thermodynamic minima by 2–3 orders of magnitude

contradiction.content: The paper reports a previously unreported oxide-dependent rare-earth inversion that contradicts the common one-RE-fits-all/single-RE practice across different oxide-forming systems, implying composition-specific or dual-RE selection instead.
evidence_spans: This oxide-dependent inversion has not been previously reported and has direct design implications: Hf should be preferred for chromia-forming alloys, while La or Y should be preferred for alumina-forming compositions. The finding challenges the common practice of applying a single RE across different oxide-forming systems without regard for oxide chemistry.
